What this verb is called. Write it in plain words - "Take Damage" becomes take_damage in the generated GDScript. Other rows call the verb by this name.
Godot's own documentation for this verb. It is written above the function as ## lines and shows up in the editor's built-in help and when hovering the verb elsewhere. Optional.

Puts a clickable button on this node's Inspector panel, labelled with whatever you type here. Pressing it runs this verb right there in the editor - handy for chores like re-baking a level or filling in test data. Leave it empty (the usual case) and no button appears.
One line saying what this verb does. It shows beside the verb in the picker, so it is what somebody reads when deciding whether this is the verb they want.
The friendly name shown in the picker instead of the function name - "Deal Damage" reads better than deal_damage. Leave it empty to let it default from the verb name.
Which section of the picker files this verb. Verbs sharing a category are grouped together, so a pack usually puts all of its verbs under one - its own name works well.
What kind of value this input accepts - a number (int / float), text (String), a true/false (bool), a position (Vector2 / Vector3), or Variant for anything at all.

An optional starting value, so whoever uses the verb can skip this input. Written as GDScript (10, 1.5, "idle", true). GDScript requires inputs WITH a default to come last, so filling this in may move the parameter down.
One line explaining this input. It shows in the picker beside the field, which is where somebody decides what to type into it.

A GDScript boolean expression - the body runs only when all hold (e.g. host.enabled).
Publishes the verb into pickers as the chosen kind.

Instantiates a scene into an off-screen viewport, lets it settle for a frame, and saves what it shows as a PNG - thumbnails, store shots, doc figures, baked sprites. Needs a windowed editor: a headless run has no renderer, so it warns and writes nothing.

Rolls a weighted table many times and reports what actually came out: per entry the rolled percent, the percent its weight implies, and the gap between them. Pure maths - it runs anywhere, and the same seed always gives the same numbers.
Runs while a project export is starting, before the files are written - the place to stamp a build number, bake a data file, or strip debug content.
Writes a small build stamp file: the version string plus the date and time the stamp was written. The timestamp is read when the tool runs, so the generated code stays identical every save.
True when the export that triggered this bake step is a debug build. Use it inside On Project Export to keep test content out of release builds.
True when the export preset that triggered this bake step carries the given feature tag - the way to bake different data for mobile, web or desktop.
Turns any value into one compact line of text a player can paste anywhere - a seed, a loadout, a whole save. Read it back with Value From Share Code.
Anything - a run seed, a loadout list, a colour, a whole save record.
Encodes any value as a share code and puts it straight on the operating system clipboard, ready to paste.
copy share code for [b]{value}[/b] to clipboard
Anything - a run seed, a loadout list, a whole save record.

True when the text really is a share code that decodes cleanly, so a paste box can refuse garbage before it reaches the game. Ask it when the pasted text CHANGES (a Paste button, On Text Changed) rather than every frame: a code mangled in transit can still reach the decoder, and the engine logs a line each time it is refused. A code that was made from nothing at all also reads as invalid.
The pasted text to test - usually Clipboard Text or a paste box's text.
Reads the value back out of a share code, giving nothing when the text is not a valid code.
The share code text to read - check it with Share Code Is Valid first.
True when the operating system clipboard currently holds any text - gate a paste box on it.
True when the operating system clipboard currently holds an image, such as a screenshot the player just copied.
The image currently on the operating system clipboard - feed it to ImageTexture.create_from_image to show it.
Compares whatever text is on the clipboard against a value, with your choice of operator.
Text to compare the clipboard against.

Copies a live node, adds the copy to a parent, places it and optionally puts it in a group - the one-row form of Duplicate Node plus Add Child plus Set Position. Use Spawn Scene when you are starting from a .tscn file instead.
World position for the copy (a Vector3 for a 3D node). Only used when the copy has a position.
Optional group for the copy (blank = none).

Copies any value aside under a name, in memory, for this run - the before-value for a preview, a buff or a cutscene. For memory that survives closing the game use Remember Between Runs on the variable, or the Save System pack.
Any label you also use in Restore Value Into.
Pours a remembered value back into a variable. When nothing was remembered under that name the variable keeps what it already had.
The label used in Remember Value As.
Variable that receives the remembered value (left alone when nothing was remembered).
The value remembered under a name this run, or your fallback when there is none - read it without pouring it back.
What you get when nothing was remembered under that name.
True when something was remembered under that name this run - the gate on a Cancel button that should only undo a preview it actually took.
Drops a remembered value, so Has Remembered reads false again. Forgetting a name that was never remembered is harmless.

Loads every data asset (.tres) in a folder as a list, so a folder of files becomes your content - items, enemies, levels, or a mod folder. A missing folder gives an empty list, and a file that fails to load is left out rather than arriving as nothing.
Folder to scan (not recursive). Every .tres / .res inside it is loaded, in the folder's own order.
Fetches one data asset out of a folder by its file name, or nothing at all when there is no such file - no red error.
File name WITHOUT the .tres extension - "rusty_sword" finds rusty_sword.tres.
Loads a file and hands back your fallback when it is missing, so a deleted or mod-supplied file never crashes the game.
Full path to the resource or scene to load.
What to use instead when the file is not there (a preloaded default, or null).
How many data assets a folder holds, counted without loading any of them - zero if the folder is missing.
Folder to count data assets in (not recursive).

Makes a private copy of a resource, right down to the resources inside it, so writing to the copy never changes the .tres on disk or any other node holding it. Use this before a node edits its own stats.
The resource to copy. Anything that is not a resource (including nothing at all) gives nothing back.

Makes a cheap copy whose own fields are separate but whose inner resources and lists are still SHARED with the original. Pick this only when you want that sharing - otherwise use Copy Resource (Independent).
Copies the array AND every list or dictionary nested inside it, so editing the copy cannot reach back into the original. Copy Array only copies the outer level.
Array variable to copy right through.
Copies the dictionary AND every list or dictionary nested inside it, so editing the copy cannot reach back into the original. Copy Dictionary only copies the outer level.
Dictionary variable to copy right through.
Pours a list of values off another object onto this one, in one row instead of one row per property. Names the target does not have are skipped, so a single preset can serve several kinds of node.
The object being written to - it is what changes.
The object to read from - a node OR a resource.
Comma-separated property names. Leave blank to copy every variable the source's script declares.

Writes a base's values ONLY into fields this object left empty, leaving everything you did fill in alone. That is the override chain: a base item plus a rarity variant, or a shipped table plus a mod file. Empty means nothing there: no value at all, blank text, an empty list or an empty record - a 0 and a false are real values and are kept, exactly as Is Nothing and Missing Fields read them.
The one being completed - it is what changes.
Where the missing values come from.
Pours a data asset's fields onto the same-named properties of a node, so difficulty tiers, weapon tunings and boss phases become a data edit instead of a wall of rows.
The data asset to pour on (a .tres you filled in the Inspector). Nothing happens if it is empty.
The node to apply it to.

True while the listed properties hold the same values on both objects - the cheap 'is this ghost still in sync' or 'has anything changed' check. A name neither object has reads as NOT matching, so a typo shows up instead of quietly passing, and either side being gone reads as not matching too.
Comma-separated property names to compare. A blank list has nothing to compare, so it is true.

True when a loaded record was written by an older build than this one - the gate a migration sits under. A record with NO version field counts as 0, so the very first format upgrades too, and so does one whose version field is empty or is not a number at all.
The parsed record (a save file, a payload, a manifest).
Which field holds the version number.
Moves a value to its new field name, and does nothing at all when the old name is not there - so a migration is safe to run twice.
The record to migrate, edited in place.
The new field name (overwritten if it is already there).
Writes the current format number onto a record, so the next load knows it has already been migrated. Data Is Older Than Version reads it back, and reads it as 0 when it is missing or is not a number.
The version this build writes - a whole number.

Reads a .csv whose FIRST line is the column names and gives you one record per row, each field reachable by column name - row["price"]. Quoted cells may contain the separator, Windows line endings are fine, and a missing file simply gives no rows. Store it in an Array variable, then walk it with a For Each pick filter.
The .csv to read. Its FIRST line must be the column names.
What separates the columns in that file.
The same column-names-first parse as Table From File, but over text you already hold instead of a file on disk.
Spreadsheet text you already have - a pasted blob, a downloaded body, a file you read earlier. FIRST line = the column names.
Gives one whole column as a list, in row order - handy for a dropdown's items, a weights list, or a quick sum. A row missing that column contributes empty text.
The rows-of-records variable a Table From File (or Table From Text) expression filled.
The column name to read, exactly as it is spelled in the header row.

Finds the FIRST record whose column holds this value - the single-item lookup, e.g. the row for item "sword". Gives an empty record when nothing matches, so check it with Dictionary Is Empty before reading fields.
The column to match on, exactly as it is spelled in the header row.
The value to look for. Compared as text, so 25 and "25" both match a cell reading 25.

Runs this event's actions once per LINE of the text, skipping blank ones. Windows (CRLF) and old-Mac (CR) endings are handled, so no line arrives with a stray carriage return. Read the current one as `line`.
The text to walk line by line - a file you read, a pasted blob, a leaderboard body.

Runs this event's actions once per PIECE of the text. Each piece arrives with its surrounding spaces trimmed, and empty pieces are skipped, so "sword; shield;; bow" is three parts. Read the current one as `part`.
for each part of [b]{text}[/b] split by [b]{separator}[/b]
The text to break up - a tag list, a chat command's arguments, one cell of a spreadsheet.
What separates the pieces, e.g. "," or ";" or " ".

Runs this event's actions once per data asset (.tres / .res) in a folder, already loaded - the "a folder of items IS my item list" setup, with no list to maintain. A folder that is not there walks nothing (quietly - it is checked first, so a loop that runs every frame cannot spam errors), and anything that fails to load is skipped rather than arriving as null. Read the current one as `entry`.
Folder of data assets to walk. Only .tres / .res files are loaded; anything else in there is ignored.
The part of the text before the first marker: Text Before("Ada [angry]: hi", " [") is "Ada". When the marker is not there you get the whole text back, so nothing is silently lost.
The line to read a piece out of.
The marker to stop at (the first one wins).
Everything after the first marker: Text After("Ada [angry]: hi", "]: ") is "hi". Empty when the marker is not there, because then there is no "after".
The marker to start after (the first one wins).
The part between two markers: Text Between("Ada [angry]: hi", "[", "]") is "angry". Empty when the opening marker is missing, and the rest of the text when the closing one is.
The first number found anywhere in the text, whole or decimal: "Chapter 3" gives 3, "v1.25-beta" gives 1.25. You get 0 when there is no number at all, and you never write a pattern.
Text that has a number somewhere in it.

Splits text on a separator but keeps anything inside "double quotes" together as one piece, and drops the quotes: give "iron sword" 2 is three pieces, not four. Empty pieces are skipped, so runs of separators never produce blanks.
The line to split - a console entry, a search box, a pasted cell.
What separates the pieces OUTSIDE quotes.

Why this JSON failed to parse, with the line: "line 4: Expected ':'". Empty when it parses fine, so an empty result IS the all-clear. Log it and the bug report writes itself. Branch on this expression's own emptiness (Text Is Blank, inverted) rather than on JSON Is Valid: that condition reads a file holding just the word null as invalid, and this one has nothing to say about it, so pairing them logs an error with a blank reason.
The JSON text to check - a file you read, a paste, a server reply.

The first cell of a table that should be a number and is not, said out loud: "row 12, column "price": "abc" is not a number". Rows are counted from 1 over the rows you hold - Table From File has already used up the header line, so row 12 is line 13 of the file. A row that is not a record at all is reported too. Empty when every listed column checks out.
A list of records - one per row, each field reachable by column name.
The columns that must hold numbers.

The listed fields that are missing or left blank, comma-separated, and empty when the record is complete. Blank means nothing there: null, empty text, an empty list or an empty record - a 0 is a real value and is never reported.
A record or a resource to check.
The fields it must have filled in, separated by commas.

Trims text to a maximum number of characters and marks the cut with the ending you choose, so a clipped name never reads as the whole name. Text that already fits comes back untouched, and the result never runs past the width you gave - a width too narrow to hold the ending simply cuts without one. Cuts mid-word: use Shorten To Whole Words when the cut should land on a word boundary.
The text that has to fit.
The widest the result may get, in characters, counting the ending below.
What marks the cut, e.g. "..." or a single ellipsis character. Its own length is taken out of the budget.

Like Shorten To Fit, but backs up to the last complete word before cutting, so "Ancient Sword of Thorns" reads "Ancient Sword..." instead of "Ancient Sword of Th". When the budget holds no whole word (one very long word) it falls back to cutting by characters, and when it is too narrow to hold the ending at all it cuts without one - so the result is never just the ending, and never wider than you asked for.

Turns a number into grouped digits a player can take in at a glance: 1234567 reads "1,234,567". Whole numbers only (the fraction is dropped); a negative keeps its minus sign. For idle-game scale (1.23e15, "1.23 Qa") reach for the Big Numbers pack instead.
The number to make readable. Anything after the decimal point is dropped.
Turns a fraction into percent TEXT with the sign on it: 0.73 reads "73%". Feed it a 0-to-1 value (Percent Of already returns 0-to-100, so divide that by 100 or use the raw fraction).
A fraction where 1.0 means full, e.g. health / max_health.
Digits after the decimal point. 0 gives a whole percent.

Seconds as a duration that survives passing an hour: 3725 reads "1h 02m" and 90 reads "1m 30s". A negative duration reads as zero. Use As Clock Time when you want strict mm:ss (it rolls an hour into "60:00").

Pads text out on the RIGHT to a fixed width, so every row starts on the same edge and reads as a column. Text longer than the width is left alone (it is never cut - shorten it first). Give the Label a MONOSPACE theme font or the column will still drift.
Column width in characters. Shorter text is padded; longer text is left as it is.
What fills the gap: a space, or "." for a dotted leader. One character.

Pads text out on the LEFT to a fixed width, so numbers END on the same edge and read as a column of figures. Text longer than the width is left alone. Give the Label a MONOSPACE theme font or the column will still drift.
The text to pad out - str() a number first.

Pads text on BOTH sides to a fixed width, so a heading sits in the middle of a column. An odd leftover space goes on the right. Text longer than the width is left alone. Give the Label a MONOSPACE theme font or the centering will still drift.

Turns a machine id into a readable name: "fire_sword" reads "Fire Sword", "maxHealth" reads "Max Health". Use it wherever a key has to be shown to a player, so ids and labels never drift apart in two places.
An id or key, e.g. fire_sword or maxHealth.
Raises the FIRST letter only and leaves the rest of the text exactly as it is, so "NPC" and "HP" keep their capitals. Empty text stays empty.
A sentence that needs its first letter raised.

Looks the whole sentence up in the current language FIRST, then fills its {slots}. The pattern you type here - slots and all - is the translation key, so it is what goes in the catalog. Filling the slots first (Translate around Text From Pattern) produces a string no catalog can contain, and the text then never translates.
The source sentence, with {name} slots. This exact string, slots and all, is the translation key that goes in the catalog.
What fills the slots: {"name": value, ...} - e.g. {"coins": coins}.

Sets this Label's text from a pattern that is translated FIRST and filled second. The pattern - slots and all - is the translation key. Re-run it under On Language Changed so the label follows a live language switch.

True when this text would convert to a number cleanly. Ask it BEFORE converting, so a typo can never arrive as a silent 0 and the sheet bet nothing. Spaces around the number are ignored; empty text is not a number.
Text to test - a typed-in field, a value read back out of a save, a CSV or JSON cell.
True when this text would convert to a WHOLE number cleanly - a count, a level, a slot index. "12" passes and "12.5" does not, which is the only difference from Text Is A Number.
Text to test - a count, a level number, a save slot, a seed.

True when the text contains at least ONE of the listed pieces - a chat filter, a keyword-triggered line, a tag-gated card. Unlike Text Is One Of, which needs the WHOLE text to equal an entry, this looks INSIDE the text. Matching is case-sensitive, and an empty list is never a match.
List of pieces to look for - written here, or a sheet variable someone can edit without touching this row.

True only when the text contains EVERY listed piece - a combo whose rule text names two keywords, a search box where all the words must match. An empty list counts as true, because nothing is missing.
List of pieces that must ALL appear.
True when the text contains none of the listed pieces - the accept-this-name branch, written as the thing you want to act on instead of an Else. An empty list always passes.
List of pieces that must NOT appear.

Reads a number out of text, or hands back the fallback YOU chose - never a surprise zero. Pair it with Text Is A Number when the two cases need different rows. The text is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
Text to read a number out of.
What you get back when the text is not a number.

Reads a whole number out of text, or hands back your fallback. "12.5" is not a whole number, so it lands on the fallback rather than quietly becoming 12 - when you want that rounding, use Number From Text and round the result yourself.
Text to read a whole number out of.
What you get back when the text is not a whole number.

True when there is nothing there: no value at all, empty text, an empty list (including an empty Split Text result), or an empty record - one row whatever the value turns out to be. A 0 is NOT nothing, because a score of zero is a real value, and neither is text made only of spaces (that is Text Is Blank).
Anything - text, a list, a record, a reference.

True when there IS something there - a name was typed, the inventory has items, the save slot was written, the item slot is filled. The exact opposite of Is Nothing, for the times the filled case is the one you want to act on.

The value when it really is a number, or your own default when it is missing, null, text, or anything else. A zero counts as a real number and is kept. Use it to put a loaded value straight into a whole-number or decimal variable without a guard row first. The value is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
The untyped value to check - a save slot read, a JSON field, a Dictionary key.
What you get back when it is not a number.

The value when it really is text with something in it, or your own default when it is missing, null, blank, or another kind of value. The classic use is a saved player name that falls back to "Player". The value is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
What you get back when it is not text, or is blank.

The value when it really is a list with items in it, or your own default when it is missing, null, empty, or another kind of value. A Split Text result counts as a list. Safe to feed straight into a For Each. The value is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
The untyped value to check - a loaded inventory, a JSON array, a Split Text result, a Dictionary key.
What you get back when it is not a list, or is empty.

The value when it really is a record (a dictionary) with keys in it, or your own default when it is missing, null, empty, or another kind of value. Pair it with Get Key so a whole missing settings block reads as defaults. The value is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
The untyped value to check - a loaded settings block, a JSON object, a Dictionary key.
What you get back when it is not a record, or is empty.

The value unless it is null, in which case your own default. This one guards nothing else: a zero, a blank text and an empty list all count as real values here. Use it for a method that can hand back null. The value is read twice in the emitted line, so keep it a plain read and not something that changes the game.
Anything that might be null - a method result, a freed reference, a missing key.
What you get back when it is null.

One named piece of a pair, a triple, a colour or a record: the up/down part of a velocity (the jump-or-fall test), the see-through part of a tint, the forward/back part of a 3D direction. Reads as a sentence instead of a typed-in .y. Pick a part the value actually has - a record that might be missing the field is the shipped Get Key (with default)'s job, because that one takes a fallback and this one does not.
A Vector2, Vector3, Color or record to read one part of.

Changes one named part and leaves the rest alone: zero the vertical speed on landing and keep the horizontal, flatten a 3D direction to the ground plane, fade only the see-through part of a tint. Writing a part a record does not have yet ADDS it.
What to change one part of: a node's own member (velocity, modulate, position) picked from the list, or the name of a sheet variable holding a Vector, Color or record.
The new value for that one part.

Checks whether a data file has been written since the last check, and fires the sheet's data_file_changed(path) signal when it has - so you edit an enemy's numbers in the Inspector and the running game picks them up. Put it under Every X Seconds; the first check only takes a reading, so nothing fires just because the row started. This is a debug-build tool: it reads the file's timestamp each time it runs.
The data file to watch (a .tres, .json or .csv).

Re-reads a data asset from disk into the copy every node is already holding, so the new numbers apply without restarting or re-assigning anything. It reloads DATA, not code: a changed script still needs a restart. Nothing happens when the path is not there.
The data asset to re-read from disk.

Runs when a Watch Data File row notices that a watched file has been written. The path arrives on the row as path, so the reaction reloads exactly the file that changed even when two land in the same check. Needs a Signal row for data_file_changed(path: String) - without one the sheet still compiles, but nothing connects this event, so it never runs. The Project Doctor flags that.
The file that was written, carried by the signal itself.

Every structural problem in a folder of data assets, one per line, and "" when it is clean: a file that cannot be loaded, one with no usable id, and two files claiming the same id (where the second quietly wins every lookup). Show it, log it, or fail a build with it.
Folder of data assets to check (not recursive).

True when every data asset in a folder loads, has an id, and has an id no sibling shares - the check to put in front of loading a mod folder or user content. Read the reasons with Data Folder Problems.

Checks a folder of data assets and writes every problem it finds to the Output as one warning, saying which file and what is wrong. A clean folder says nothing at all, so it is safe to leave in a startup event.

Where a world point sits on screen right now, camera zoom and scroll included - pin a nameplate, a health bar or a damage number to something that moves. Put the answer on a node that lives on a CanvasLayer and it will track its target without lagging behind the camera.
A position in the game world.
The world position under a screen pixel - click-to-place, a gamepad cursor, a HUD marker dragged onto the map. The exact opposite of World Point To Screen, so the two round-trip.
A position in screen pixels, with 0,0 at the top-left of the view.

Where a 3D world point lands on screen - nameplates over 3D characters, damage numbers, objective pins drawn on a CanvasLayer. Reads as 0,0 while there is no active 3D camera, so it never faults during a scene change. Check Is Behind Camera (3D) first: a point behind you still projects to a number.
True while a world point is inside the visible view - the honest gate for spawning, culling, showing an off-screen arrow, or holding a tutorial callout until its subject is actually visible.
Pixels of slack outside the view that still count as on screen. Negative pulls the test inward.

True when a 3D point sits behind the camera plane, where its projected screen position is a mirrored lie. The guard every 3D waypoint marker needs before it draws. With no camera in the scene it reads true, so nothing is drawn into a view that does not exist.

A screen position that follows a target while it is visible and sticks to the edge of the view once it is not - the off-screen objective arrow, the radar blip, the "your teammate is over there" chevron. Pair it with Marker Angle Toward for the rotation.
How far in from the edge the marker is parked.

The rotation in degrees an on-screen arrow needs so it points from the middle of the view at a world thing - the other half of the off-screen marker, and it stays right while the camera zooms or rotates.

The rectangle of the world the camera can currently see, in world coordinates - spawn just outside it, cull outside it, clamp a node inside it, or size a minimap to it. Follows the camera's zoom and position with nothing to keep in sync.

The Asteroids rule in 3D: leave the right of the view and come back on the left, off the top and back at the bottom, at the same distance from the camera. The missing twin of the 2D Wrap Inside The Screen, for a wrap-around arena or an endless shoal. Does nothing while there is no 3D camera.
An evenly spread random point inside a circle - the sqrt weighting is done for you, so scatter does not bunch up in the middle the way the obvious version does.
A random point exactly ON the rim of a circle, never inside it - a spawn ring around the player, orbiting decor, a radial menu slot, the starting point of a homing shot.
random point on a circle of [b]{radius}[/b] around [b]{center}[/b]

A random point in the doughnut between two radii - the off-screen spawner that never drops an enemy in the player's lap, and never so far away it never arrives. Evenly spread across the whole band, not crowded against the inner edge.

A random point inside an axis-aligned rectangle - loot scatter across a room, prop placement, confetti over a banner, a patrol target inside a zone. Feed it Visible World Rect's position and size to scatter across whatever the camera can see.
random point in the rect at [b]{top_left}[/b] sized [b]{size}[/b]
A random point inside a wedge - shotgun spread, cone attacks, directional scatter, a spray of sparks away from a wall. Facing and spread are in degrees, so the row reads the way you think about it.
random point in a [b]{spread_degrees}[/b] cone facing [b]{facing_degrees}[/b] from [b]{center}[/b]
Direction the wedge points, in degrees.
Total width of the cone in degrees, half either side of facing.

Random scatter around a node that is already in the scene - blood splats around a hit, footprints around a stomp, sparkles around a pickup, a wander target around home. Pick the node instead of typing its position, and the scatter follows it as it moves.
Node the point is scattered around.
A random unit direction in 2D - multiply it by a speed for a random shove, by a distance for a random offset. Always exactly one unit long, so the strength stays where you set it.
A random unit direction in 3D, evenly spread over the whole sphere. The naive three-random-numbers version crowds the corners of a cube; this one does not, so debris and shrapnel fly out honestly.
An evenly spread random point inside a 3D sphere - spawn clouds, debris fields, flocking targets. The cube-root weighting keeps the middle from filling up first.
A random point inside an axis-aligned 3D box - scatter trees over a chunk, spawn enemies in a room volume, place ambient audio emitters. Size is the FULL box, measured around the centre.
random point in a [b]{size}[/b] box at [b]{center}[/b]

A random WORLD position on the border of what the camera can see - the wave spawner that comes in from a random side, ambient wildlife entering the frame, a meteor starting its run. Grow it with Visible World Rect if you want them to appear from just outside.
random point on the screen edge

Nudges a value by a random amount up to the size you give - pitch variation on a sound, a pixel or two of scatter on a decal, a shade of variation on a tint. Works on numbers, vectors and colors as long as the amount is the same kind of value.
The number, vector or color being nudged.
The most it can move, as the SAME kind of value - a number for a number, a Vector2 for a position, a Color for a tint.
The velocity a moving thing has AFTER hitting a surface - feed it the normal any hit trigger or raycast hands you. Ricochets, pinball, breakout, deflect shields.
How the thing was moving when it hit.
The normal any hit trigger or raycast hands you.
1 keeps all the speed, 0.6 is a rubber ball, 0 is a dead stop.

The velocity left over once the part pushing INTO a surface is removed - a wall slide that keeps you moving along the wall instead of sticking to it, slope movement, a dash that grazes a corner rather than stopping dead.
How the thing was moving when it met the surface.
The heading in degrees a thing travels on after bouncing off a surface - the answer to feed straight back into Set Angle Of Motion when a bullet should ricochet instead of dying.
The heading it was travelling on, in degrees.

A position just clear of a surface instead of exactly on it - park a ricocheting bullet, a decal or a spawned effect here. Landing exactly on a surface is how a thing ends up stuck inside it on the next frame, because a ray that starts inside a shape does not report it.
Pixels of daylight to leave between the thing and the surface.

Turns this node to point the way it is travelling, and leaves it alone while it is standing still so a stopped thing never snaps back to facing right. Arrows, fish, cars, thrown knives, a camera that leads the motion.
How this node is moving - Get Velocity on a body, or the direction you are driving it with.

Turns a 3D node to face a point WITHOUT the crash the plain Look At has: when the target is directly overhead or underfoot, the usual up vector points the same way as the look direction and Godot cannot build a rotation from that. This one swaps the up vector at the last moment, and does nothing at all when the target is where the node already is.

Turns a 3D node to face a point but only around the up axis, so a character looks at the player without tipping over to stare at their feet. The rotation every humanoid, turret base and standing NPC actually wants.

Where to aim so a shot MEETS a moving target instead of trailing it - the interception point every turret and archer needs. When the target is faster than the shot no lead exists, and it falls back to the target's current spot rather than pointing somewhere absurd.
Where the target is right now.
How the target is moving, in pixels per second.
How fast your shot travels, in pixels per second.

The angle in degrees to fire something so it ARCS onto a target - grenades, mortars, catapults, a coin tossed into a counter. Picks the flatter of the two possible arcs, and reads as 45 degrees when the shot cannot reach at all, so a row never produces a number that is not a number.
launch angle to reach [b]{distance}[/b] away, [b]{height}[/b] up
How far away the target is, along the ground.
How much higher the target is than the launcher; negative is downhill.
How fast the thing leaves the launcher.
Pull downward, in the same units as the speed.

How many seconds something moving at a steady speed needs to cover a distance - time a warning before the missile lands, size a tween to match a walk, decide whether the interceptor can get there first.

Which grid cell a world position falls in - no TileMapLayer needed, so build grids, inventory slots and chunk keys all speak the same language. Negative positions land in negative cells, which is what a grid that extends left and up actually wants.
Pixels across one cell. Type Tiles(1) to read your project's own tile size instead.
The world position at the middle of a grid cell - where the placement ghost sits, where the tower is built, where the piece lands. The exact partner of Cell Of Point, so the pair round-trips.
center of cell [b]{cell}[/b] on a [b]{cell_size}[/b] grid

The nearest grid intersection to a loose position - a dragged card falling into its slot, a level editor brush, a UI element clicking onto a column. Rounds to the nearest, so a thing dropped just past halfway moves forward rather than back.
The nearest point on a 3D grid - voxel placement, modular level pieces clicking together, a build cursor that lines up with the floor tiles.

How far apart two grid cells are, with the same geometry dropdown the rest of the plugin uses: straight line, horizontal or vertical only, grid steps (Manhattan) or king moves (Chebyshev). One expression that fits a roguelike, a strategy game and a puzzle board alike.
distance from cell [b]{from_cell}[/b] to [b]{to_cell}[/b], measured as [b]{metric}[/b]
How the distance is counted - a roguelike wants Grid steps, a chess board wants King moves.

The cells touching a cell, as a list - flood fill, path search, "is anything next to me", spreading fire, match-three clearing. Choose four sides, eight including diagonals, or the six neighbours of an axial hex board.
The cell whose neighbours you want.
How cells touch on this board.

Every cell a straight line passes through, in order from one cell to the other - a laser beam's path, tile-based line of sight, a corridor carved between two rooms, a ruler for a ranged attack. Both ends are included.
cells in the line from [b]{from_cell}[/b] to [b]{to_cell}[/b]

Every cell within a step radius of a centre cell, as a list - a blast footprint, a range preview, a fog reveal, the tiles a tower covers. Choose the diamond (counting grid steps) or the square (counting king moves).
How many steps out from the middle.

Every cell in a rectangular block, row by row - stamping a room, laying out an inventory grid, placing a multi-cell building, clearing a region of fog. An empty or negative size walks nothing rather than looping backwards.
How many cells across and down.

True while a cell is on the board - the guard before every placement, every move and every array lookup keyed by cell. Counting starts at 0,0 in the top-left, so a 20 by 12 board's last cell is 19,11.
How many cells the board is across and down.
Runs this event's actions once per cell within a step radius of a centre cell - range previews, blast footprints, fog reveal, area-of-effect highlights. Read the current one as `cell`.

How strong an effect is at a distance, from 1 at the centre to 0 at the edge - the one number that makes an explosion, a sound, a magnet or a screen shake care how close it was. Anything past the radius reads as 0, so it is safe to multiply straight into damage. For a hand-drawn profile, feed this number into Sample Curve.
How quickly the strength drops off with distance.

Falloff between THIS node and another one, without spelling out either position - guard suspicion that builds faster the closer you are, a magnet that pulls harder up close, a sound that ducks as you approach. Reads 0 once the other node is out of range.
The node the strength is measured against.
Throws this physics body away from a blast, weaker the further it was - barrels, crates, ragdolls and debris flung by an explosion. One row on the body; the blast only has to say where it happened.
The push at the very centre, in impulse units.
Past this the push is nothing.

Shoves every member of a group away from a point, hardest at the centre and not at all past the radius - the mirror of Pull Group Toward. A shockwave clearing a crowd, a repulsor field, a dash that parts the enemies it passes through.
Only members inside this are shoved.
Pixels the closest member is moved.

True while a point sits inside a facing wedge - guard vision, spotlight checks, melee arcs, directional blasts. The cheap test to put in front of an expensive raycast: if it is not in the cone, there is nothing to trace.
[b]{point}[/b] is within a [b]{fov_degrees}[/b] cone of [b]{origin}[/b] facing [b]{facing_degrees}[/b]
Tip of the wedge - the guard, the spotlight, the blast.
Which way the wedge points, in degrees.
Total width of the wedge in degrees.
How far the wedge extends, in pixels.

Pauses this event until a check comes true, or until the give-up time passes. Read which happened on the next row with Wait Succeeded / Wait Timed Out, naming this wait. It polls once a frame, so prefer Wait For Signal when a real signal exists for what you are waiting on.
A name for this wait, so Wait Succeeded / Wait Timed Out can say which one they mean.
The check to wait for, tested once a frame.
Seconds before giving up. 0 waits forever.

Pauses this event until every signal in the list has fired at least once, or until the give-up time passes. It connects them ALL up front, one-shot, so nothing can fire into the gap between two waits - the bug a hand-written chain of awaits always has. An empty list succeeds at once.
wait [b]{wait_name}[/b] for ALL of [b]{signals}[/b], give up after [b]{seconds}[/b]s
The signals to join, as a list: [$Door.opened, $Camera.arrived].

Pauses this event until the first of several signals fires, then carries on - a race, or a sudden-death timer. Read which one won with First To Finish, naming this wait: it answers "Node.signal", so racing $Player.died against $Boss.died still tells you which one it was. Every signal is connected one-shot up front, so the winner is whichever really fired first, and the losers are disconnected when the race ends.
A name for this wait, so First To Finish and the outcome conditions can say which one they mean.
The signals to race, as a list: [$Player.died, $Boss.died].
True when the named wait ended because what it was waiting for happened. A wait that has never run is neither succeeded nor timed out, so nothing fires before the wait does.
The name the wait row used.

True when the named wait gave up instead of finishing - the recovery branch for a load that never reported in. The same timeout also reports on verb_failed, so another event can handle it as On Failure Of.

Which signal a Wait For Any Of was watching finished first, written as "Node.signal" (the node's name, a dot, the signal's name), or empty text when it timed out. The node is part of the answer on purpose: a race between $Player.died and $Boss.died is two signals with the same name, and only the owner tells them apart. Compare it in a condition cell to branch on the winner.
The name the Wait For Any Of row used.

Runs this event's actions over and over, up to a number of attempts, so a nested Stop Retrying can end it the moment the thing works. With no waiting inside it stays instant, which makes it the procedural-placement loop as much as the disk retry. Read the try number with Retry Attempt Number.
A name for this retry, matching its Stop Retrying and Retries Exhausted rows.

Which try this is, counting from 1 - the number you put in the log line or the HUD. Only readable inside a Retry Up To N Times loop, and it reads that loop's own variable, so change the cell if you renamed it.
The retry loop's own variable. Leave it as attempt unless you renamed the loop variable on the Retry Up To N Times row.
Ends the retry loop right now because the attempt worked, and records that it worked so Retries Exhausted below stays false. Put it under the condition that means success.
The name the Retry Up To N Times row uses.

True when the retry loop above ran out of tries without a Stop Retrying - the give-up branch. Put it in a sibling row directly beneath the retry loop, using the same name; a retry that has never run is not exhausted, so nothing fires before the loop does. Reading it clears the record, so the next run starts clean. When the retry WAITS between tries (Wait Before Next Try) the loop is still running while the rows beneath it are reached, so report that give-up with Report Failure on the last attempt and handle it in an On Failure Of event instead.

Pauses before the next attempt, waiting longer each time when you set a growth above 1 - the polite way to retry a disk or a slow source. It suspends this event like Wait does, so pair the retry with Once At A Time when the trigger can fire again mid-retry.
Wait after the first failed try.
1 = the same wait every time, 2 = doubling backoff.
Which try this is - put Retry Attempt Number here.
Records a value into a named rolling history you can dump, chart, or check when something goes wrong.
The value to record this tick - a number, a vector, anything printable.
Trail name - any label you also use in the trail expressions.
How many recent values to hold (older ones drop off the front).
Returns the whole trail as an array, oldest first - feed it to a chart, a table, or an array action.
Trail name, matching a Remember In Trail action.
The smallest value recorded in a trail, which is the spike a per-frame watch blinked past. An empty trail reads as INF.
The largest value recorded in a trail. An empty trail reads as -INF.
The mean of every number recorded in a trail - a rolling average that is as useful in gameplay as in debugging. An empty trail reads as 0.
The most recently recorded value in a trail, or 0 when nothing has been recorded yet.
How many values a trail is currently holding, which tops out at the Keep you gave it.
Prints the whole trail to the Output console, so the seconds before a bug arrive with the bug.
Writes a trail to a two-column CSV file you can open in a spreadsheet and plot.
Where to write the file. Use user:// so it works in an exported game.
Forgets everything a trail recorded, so the next run starts from nothing.
True on a frame that took longer than your budget, which is the hitch caught as it happens. Needs a per-frame trigger.
The budget. 16.6 is one frame at 60 FPS.
True once the framerate has stayed under your floor for the whole stretch you name, which tells a real performance drop apart from one stuttery frame. Needs a per-frame trigger.
The framerate floor. Below this counts as a drop.
How long the drop must last before this is true.
Starts a named stopwatch. Pair it with Stop Measuring around the work you suspect.
The name this measurement is reported under.
Stops a named stopwatch and files the result, keeping the last, the average and the worst reading for that name.
The name you gave Start Measuring.
How many milliseconds the most recent run of a named measurement took.
The mean cost in milliseconds across every run of a named measurement, which is the number to quote when you claim an optimization worked.
The worst run of a named measurement in milliseconds, which is usually the one the player felt.
Prints every named measurement taken so far with its last, average and peak cost - the report you paste into a bug or a devlog.
Throws away every measurement recorded so far, so a fresh run starts from a clean slate.

Publishes this node under a short name anything can ask for, so no other row needs a path to it. Run it under On Ready. Registering the same name again replaces it, and a freed node answers as nothing at all, so a scene reload leaves no dangling reference behind.
A role, not a class - "player", "audio_director", "wallet". Registering the same name again replaces it.
The node published under a name, or nothing at all when nobody registered it or it has been freed. Drop it wherever a node is asked for - it never crashes and never needs a path.
The name the node registered itself under.
True when a node is registered under this name and is still alive. Guard an optional system with it - a missing audio director then costs you a skipped row instead of a crash.
The service name to test for.

Runs this event's actions once per node ANYWHERE in the tree that answers to a method name - the save sweep, the pause sweep, the shutdown sweep, with no list to keep in step. It walks the whole tree, so run it on an event, not every frame. Read the current one as `node`.
The method name a node must have to be picked up, e.g. save_state or on_game_paused.

Runs one action once the frame's physics and signal storm has finished, which is the only safe moment to add, free or reparent nodes. The number one crash a beginner hits is doing that from inside a collision callback; this is the fix, and the rows below it still run immediately.
The action to run once this frame's work is finished - the only safe moment to add, free or reparent a node.

Runs one action after a delay, with no Timer node and WITHOUT suspending - the rows below it keep running. The connection is one-shot, so a delayed beat can neither leak nor fire twice. The readable form of the small follow-up: eject the shell, close the door, play the second thud.
Seconds to wait before the action runs.
The action to run when the delay is up.

Sets a property at the end of the frame instead of right now. The one Godot insists on for collision shapes and monitoring: flipping those mid-physics is the error every beginner meets, and deferring is the documented answer.
set [b]{property}[/b] of [i]{target}[/i] to [b]{value}[/b] after this frame
Name of the property to set.
The value to set it to.

True the FIRST time it is reached in a frame under this name, and false for every other time that frame - counting a physics tick as its own frame, so a row under On Physics Process is not folded in with the drawn frame around it. Fifty inventory changes then rebuild the panel once instead of fifty times. Give two rows the same name and they share one run per frame.
The gate's name. Every row using the same name folds into one run per frame.

Spawns a scene under a name, sets a record of values on it before it enters the tree, and remembers it under that name so every later row can say The Spawned. If the sheet declares a scene_spawned(spawn_name, node) signal, this fires it with both, so another event can react to the new node without ever asking what was spawned last.
A name for this spawn, so later rows can say The Spawned "boss".
Values to set as it arrives, as a record: {"max_health": 200, "tier": 3}. Names the scene does not have are set anyway, so keep to its own fields.
The node to add it under. Leave as nothing to add it under this one.

Brings one of the editor's top tabs to the front - the same click as pressing 2D or Script yourself.
Which of the editor's top tabs to bring forward.
Reveals a folder or file in the editor's project file list and selects it - what a tool does after it writes something, so the reader can see what just landed.
The folder or file to reveal, as a res:// path.
Jumps the script editor to a line of the script it already has open - how a tool points at the thing it is complaining about.
The line to jump to, counted from zero.
Puts a window or dialog under the editor's own root, which is what makes it show up with the editor's theme and stay on top of it. Free it again when the plugin is disabled.
Add window {window} to the editor's root
The window or dialog to hang on the editor.
Adds one entry to the editor's command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), so a tool is reachable without a menu of its own.
The words the command palette shows.
The unique key the palette files it under.
The function to run when the command is chosen.
Adds a tab to the row Output and Debugger share, at the bottom of the editor. Remove it on plugin disabled or the row keeps a tab nobody owns.
The Control to show in the bottom row.
The words on its tab, beside Output and Debugger.
Takes the plugin's tab back out of the bottom row.
The Control that was added to the bottom row.
Runs whenever the project's files change on disk - something was imported, moved, deleted or added. The place to rescan whatever a tool keeps a list of.
Runs when the user changes anything in Editor Settings. Re-read the preferences a tool draws with, so it follows the theme instead of keeping the old one.
Moves a 3D node along one of its own directions - forward, back, right, left, up or down - at a speed a second.
Which of its own six directions to move along.
Turns a 3D node about its up axis - the yaw a character or a turret turns with.
Degrees a second, turning clockwise seen from above; a negative number turns the other way.
Tilts a 3D node's nose up or down - the pitch a plane or a camera arm moves with.
Degrees a second; a negative number tilts the other way.
Rolls a 3D node about the way it faces - the bank a plane or a ship leans with.
Degrees a second; a negative number rolls the other way.
Turns a 3D node smoothly toward a facing instead of snapping to it - the way a turret leads its target.
The facing to turn toward - Facing Along a direction gives you one.
How fast it closes the gap, per second. Bigger turns harder.
The facing that looks along a direction - what Rotate Toward Facing turns toward.
Puts a 3D node exactly where another one is - how a spawn point, a socket or a respawn marker is used.
The object to stand where - a spawn marker, a socket, another character.
Tilts a 3D node so its up points the way the ground does - the line that makes a dropped crate sit flat on a hill.
The way the surface faces - a ray hit gives you one as its `normal`.
Asks whether something is inside the cone this object is looking down - a vision cone, a backstab check, an aim assist.
The way this object faces. Its own forward, unless you say otherwise.
The direction to the thing being looked for - Direction To gives you one.
Half the width of the cone, in degrees. 45 is a 90-degree field of view.
Asks whether a place is behind this object - the backstab half of a facing test.
Asks whether a place is in front of this object, whichever way it happens to be turned.
Asks whether a place is off this object's right side - which way to lean, dodge or steer.
Asks whether a place is off this object's left side - the twin of Is To The Right Of.
The point an angle and a distance name. Add it to a centre for a place on a circle; grow the distance every tick and it draws a spiral.
Places a number of copies evenly around a circle - the bullet-hell ring, the radial menu, the circle of pillars.
Create [b]{count}[/b] of {scene} evenly around a circle of [i]{radius}[/i]
How far out from the centre they sit.
Reads a place back the other way - as the angle from one point to another and how far apart they are, both named in one drop.
True while the mouse is pointing at this object in the 3D world - hover highlights, tooltips and "what am I about to click" all start here. Needs an active Camera3D.
The object the cursor has to be over for this to be true.
Which collision layers the ray may see, by the names this project gave them.
How far into the scene the ray reaches, in metres.
Fires when a mouse button goes down over this object in the 3D world - click-to-select, click-to-attack, click-to-open. Lives in an input event, beside the other On ... pressed rows.
The object the click has to land on.
The world point on the floor the cursor is aiming at - where to drop a build ghost, a move-order marker or a decal.
The world point on the floor the cursor is aiming at - where to drop a build ghost, a move-order marker or a decal. Aimed through a crosshair object rather than the OS pointer.
The crosshair or virtual cursor to aim through. Its position ON THE CANVAS is what aims the ray, so a gamepad or touch cursor works exactly like the pointer.
The floor object the cursor is aiming at, or nothing when the cursor is off the floor.
The floor object the cursor is aiming at, or nothing when the cursor is off the floor. Aimed through a crosshair object rather than the OS pointer.
Which way the floor faces under the cursor - hand it to Align To The Ground's Slope, or ask Slope Steeper Than whether it is buildable.
Which way the floor faces under the cursor - hand it to Align To The Ground's Slope, or ask Slope Steeper Than whether it is buildable. Aimed through a crosshair object rather than the OS pointer.
True when the ground faces further than this from straight up - the buildable test a placement preview tints itself with.
Which way the ground faces - the floor slope expressions answer exactly this.
How far from flat counts as too steep.
Where this object is ON THE CANVAS, in pixels. Camera zoom and canvas layers are already in the answer, which is exactly what plain position arithmetic gets wrong.
The object being asked where it is on screen.
Where this 3D object lands ON THE CANVAS, in pixels - the number a health bar over its head, an off-screen arrow or an aim assist is positioned by.
The 3D object being asked where it is on screen.
The middle of what the player can see, in pixels - where a crosshair sits.

Walks the instances and keeps whichever is closest to a point ON THE CANVAS - aim assist, snap-to-target crosshairs and "whichever one I am nearly pointing at". Measured in pixels, so camera zoom is honoured; anything behind the camera is skipped.
pick nearest of [i]{list}[/i] to canvas point {from} -> [b]{name}[/b]
The name the one it picks goes by in the rows below. Nothing is picked when the list is empty or everything is off screen, so check the name exists first.
The instances to pick from - usually a group, which is how a project spells "every one of this kind".
The canvas point distances are measured from, in pixels. The canvas centre is the crosshair.
How far from that point, in PIXELS, still counts. Nothing beyond it is picked.
Detaches a child node from this one without deleting it, so you can reattach it later.
Child to detach (by index here - no hardcoded name; pick one or use a scene-unique node). Not freed.

Moves a node that is already in the layout under a new parent - picking an item up into a hand, mounting a rider on a saddle, holstering a weapon on a back. Keeping its place leaves it exactly where it looks; snapping to it puts it at the parent's own spot.
The node that becomes a child. It keeps everything it is - only its parent changes.
Whether the child stays where it is in the world, or snaps to its new parent.

Takes a node off whatever it is under and puts it back at the top of the layout, keeping the place it has in the world - dropping a carried item, dismounting a rider. The node is not freed and nothing else about it changes.
The node to take off its parent. It stays in the layout, at the top level.

Stops a child moving, turning and scaling with its parent while leaving it a child in every other way - it is still freed with the parent and still picked as one of its children. The answer for a muzzle flash that should not swing with the gun, or a health bar that should not tilt with the enemy.
The child that should stop (or start) following its parent.
On: the child stays where it is when the parent moves.

Points a RemoteTransform at the node it should drive, so that node follows this one without being its child at all. Which parts follow - position, angle, size - are the RemoteTransform's own switches.
The RemoteTransform2D / RemoteTransform3D doing the copying.
Path to the node its place is copied onto.
Clears a RemoteTransform's target, so whatever it was driving stops following immediately. The node it drove keeps the place it had.
The RemoteTransform2D / RemoteTransform3D to switch off.

Runs this event's actions once per direct child of a node - healing a squad, totting up an inventory, checking every socket. Read the current one as `child`. Children added while it runs are not visited by this pass.
The node whose children the actions run once for.
Reorders a child to a new sibling index, changing its draw and process order.
Child to reorder (by index here - no hardcoded name; pick one or use a scene-unique node).
Safely deletes a node at the end of the frame, e.g. removing a dead enemy.
Node to free at the end of the frame.
Runs when a child node is added beneath this one, e.g. reacting to spawned items.
Runs just before a child node leaves this one - while it is still there to be read, so a count, a total or a panel can be brought up to date with it.
Puts one item in a menu. The id is how the menu says which item was picked, so On Item Chosen answers the same number this row was given.
Runs when the user picks the item with this id out of the menu. Every item of one menu shares a single handler, so all of them stay together in the emitted file.
The menus a tool puts on screen: the items that go in one, and the event that runs when the user picks one of them.
The menu variable this row acts on - the one the menu was made into.
The words the item shows in the menu.
The number this item sends when it is chosen. Give every item its own - two items sharing one id means the second one can never run.
The id of the item this event answers - the same number Add Item gave it.

Which 2D body or area the mouse is over, or nothing when it is over empty space - click-to-select, hover highlights and "what am I about to pick up". Asked as a point query, so overlapping shapes answer with the one on top.
Which collision layers the query may see, by the names this project gave them.

Which cell of a tilemap layer the mouse is over, as map coordinates - the number Set Tile At, Erase Tile At and Cell Is Empty all take. Tile painting, build grids and "which square did I click" start here.
The tilemap layer the cell is looked up in. Its own transform is what turns the pointer into a cell, so a scrolled or zoomed map answers correctly.
Dropping it on the canvas offers the secrets counter.
%s is marked a secret. Add the event that counts it the first time the player walks in?
Show the control's key on a label while the window is open
Clear the prompt off its label as the window shuts
The label that shows the prompt, as a node path - $PromptLabel.
Every colour set this palette asset carries, side by side.
Which way something faces. Mirror or flip a sprite, a whole object with its hitbox and its ray, a 3D model, a UI panel, the camera's view, one tile, or a path - each host in its own honest terms.
Mirror it horizontally (facing left), or put it back the way it was.
Turn it upside down, or put it back the right way up.
Act on another node instead of this one. Leave blank for this node, pick a node, or address one without a tree path - e.g. get_tree().get_first_node_in_group("player").
The value holding how fast this object is moving.
The child that must stay readable - a name plate, a health bar, a damage number.
Mirrors this node's picture left-to-right - the way a 2D character faces.
Turns this node's picture upside down, or puts it back the right way up.
True while this node's picture is mirrored - which way the character is facing.
True while this node's picture is upside down.
Mirrors this object AND everything under it - the picture, the hitbox, the muzzle point and the ray all face the same way.
True while this object is mirrored, read off its own X scale.
Mirrors a 3D object along X. Worth knowing: a negative scale flips the mesh's winding, so lighting and backface culling see it inside out - Turn Around is usually what you want instead.
Mirrors a 3D label along X - readable backwards, which is the point when it is a decal or a sign seen from behind.
True while this 3D object is mirrored along X.
Turns a 3D object to face the other way - half a turn about its up axis. The honest 3D answer to mirroring: nothing is inside out afterwards.
Faces the way this object is moving, and leaves it facing that way when it stops - the one line every platformer writes by hand.
Turns this object to face another one - an enemy looking at the player, a shopkeeper looking at whoever walked in.
Re-negates a child's X scale so it does NOT come along when this object mirrors - what keeps a name plate readable instead of writing it backwards.
Mirrors a UI element in place. The pivot is moved to its middle first, which is the half everyone forgets - without it the panel mirrors AND jumps sideways.
True while this UI element is mirrored.
Mirrors everything this camera sees - a mirror world, a reflection, a level played backwards.
Mirrors what a sub-viewport shows - the rear-view mirror, the security monitor, the reflection in the water.
Mirrors the tile already sitting at a cell, keeping its tileset and its tile - how one wall art asset covers both sides of a corridor.
Mirrors every point of this path about x = 0 - the second half of a symmetric level, or a patrol route reused facing the other way.
an object is mirrored to face the way it moves, and its ray, its spawn points and its particles turn with it
Name the key and dropping it on the canvas offers the door event. Leave it blank for a door that is not locked.
%s wants the %s key. Add the event that tries it when the player walks in?
Trying %s when the player walks in.
steers the run in the air, keeps the rest
a sine wave, as you move
Keys and the doors that want them
Enemies noticing you, and each other
what this object rides, and can let go of
A skill tree - prerequisites, points and unlocks
